summary: Chogye Trichen Rinpoche (1920–2007) was a scholar in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He studied under traditional teachers Kunga Chophel, Zimwok Rinpoche, and Geshe Tshechok (1929), and later taught Cyrus Stearns, Warren Lee Todd, and David P. Jackson, among others.
Chogyū Takayama (1871–1902) worked in philosophy, Japanology, and other fields. He studied at Fukushima Prefectural Asaka High School (~1887–1891) and the University of Tokyo (~1893–1896).
Chokgyur Dechen Lingpa (1829–1870) was a scholar in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He studied under Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and Jamgön Kongtrul Lodrö Thaye, the latter of whom he also taught.

Chokyi Nyima Rinpoche (born 1951) works in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He studied at Rumtek Monastery and under numerous teachers, including the 16th Karmapa and Dilgo Khyentse. He founded the Rangjung Yeshe Institute (1981) and became abbot of Ka-Nying Shedrub Ling (1976).
Chong Go is a Buddhist studies scholar. He studied at Dongguk University and under the traditional teacher Daehaeng (attested 2012).
Chris Clark is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology. He completed his PhD at the University of Sydney under Mark Allon by 2015, where he later served as an honorary associate (attested 2019).

Christian August Brandis (1790–1867) was a scholar in philosophy and history/archaeology who studied at Kiel University (~1808–1812). He held posts at the University of Copenhagen (~1812–1815), Humboldt University of Berlin (~1816–1821), and the University of Bonn (~1821–1867).

Christian Bartholomae (1855–1925) specialized in Iranian and Central Asian studies, linguistics, and Indology, studying under Heinrich Hübschmann (~1877–1879). He held posts at Halle-Wittenberg (~1879–1885), Münster (~1885–1898), Giessen (~1898–1900), and Heidelberg (~1909–1924).

Christian Bernert is a scholar in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He studied at the International Buddhist Academy and the University of Vienna, where he completed his Magister degree under MA supervisor Klaus-Dieter Mathes.

Christian Coseru is a scholar of philosophy, Buddhist studies, and Indology. He earned his BA and MA at the University of Bucharest and his PhD at the Australian National University (~1999–2003). In ~2006, he became Associate Professor at the College of Charleston.

Christian Gottlob Heyne (1729–1812) was a scholar of linguistics and history/archaeology who earned a master's at Leipzig University (1748–1752). He was appointed professor at the University of Göttingen (1763) and served as director of Göttingen State and University Library (1764–1812).

Christian Haskett specializes in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology. He completed a PhD at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (attested 2010), advised by Robert A. F. Thurman and Michael Chamberlain, and held a post at Washington and Lee University (attested 2010).

Christian K. Wedemeyer (born 1969) works in Buddhist studies, religious studies, and Indology. He earned his MA and PhD at Columbia University under Robert A. F. Thurman, and later taught at the University of Copenhagen (2000–2003) and the University of Chicago (~2003).

Christian Karl Josias von Bunsen (1791–1860) was a scholar of religious studies and linguistics. He studied at Marburg, Göttingen (under Christian Gottlob Heyne), Munich, Leiden, and Copenhagen, and under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy in 1816. He founded the German Archaeological Institute (1829).

Christian Lassen (1800–1876) was a scholar of Indology and linguistics. After studying at Oslo, Heidelberg, and Bonn (under August Wilhelm Schlegel), he served at the University of Bonn as Privatdozent (1830) and professor of Old Indian language and literature (1840–1876).

Christian Lee Novetzke (born 1969) works in Indology, religious studies, and history/archaeology. He studied at Macalester College, Harvard, and Columbia University. He taught at the University of Pennsylvania (2003–2007) before becoming a professor at the University of Washington in 2007.

Christian Lindtner (1953–2020) was a scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology. He completed his doctoral degree at the University of Copenhagen by 1982 and served there as a professor (attested 1980–1991).

Christian Luczanits specializes in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and Indology. He earned his Magister (1994) and PhD (1998) at the University of Vienna, and held posts as a curator at the Rubin Museum of Art (attested 2012) and visiting professor at Stanford and UC Berkeley.

Christian Wittern is a scholar in Sinology and Buddhist studies who studied under Seizan Yanagida. He held posts at Kyoto University (attested 1993, 2008), where he was a professor, and at Hanazono University (attested 2011).

Christianus Cornelis Uhlenbeck (1866–1951) was a scholar of linguistics and Indology. He studied at Stedelijk Gymnasium Haarlem and Leiden University (~1883–1888), subsequently holding professorial posts at the University of Amsterdam (1892–1899) and Leiden University (1899–1926).
